qs.q: What is the primary source of restriction enzymes used in molecular biology laboratories?
qs.e: Restriction enzymes are part of the bacterial defense system against phages. They are not derived from mammalian cell cultures, which are used for other purposes.

qs.q: A molecular biology researcher is studying a DNA sample that exhibits a left-handed helix with a zig-zag appearance and 12 base pairs per turn. Which DNA conformation is this?
qs.e: Z-DNA is characterized by a left-handed helix, a zig-zag appearance, and 12 base pairs per turn. B-DNA and A-DNA both possess right-handed helical twists.

qs.q: A molecular biology student is examining prokaryotic translation termination factors. Which specific prokaryotic release factor recognizes the stop codons UAA and UAG?
qs.e: In prokaryotes, RF-1 is responsible for recognizing stop codons UAA and UAG, whereas RF-2 recognizes UAA and UGA. eRF is the eukaryotic release factor.

qs.q: A biochemistry student is reviewing the properties of transfer RNA molecules involved in protein synthesis. If a tRNA molecule has not yet been linked to any amino acid, how is it formally designated in molecular biology?
o: Initiator tRNA, used to start protein synthesis.
Uncharged tRNA, lacking any attached amino acid.
Hydrolyzed tRNA, whose amino acid has been removed by hydrolysis.
Mischarged tRNA, bearing an incorrect amino acid.
qs.e: A tRNA molecule without an attached amino acid is called an uncharged tRNA. A mischarged tRNA refers to one mistakenly attached to the wrong amino acid.

qs.q: Which two scientific disciplines are bridged by molecular biology to provide insights into heredity and cellular function?
qs.e: Molecular biology bridges genetics and biochemistry to uncover how molecular components contribute to life. Anatomy and physiology are broader medical sciences that do not define the core foundation of molecular biology in this context.
qs.s: Molecular Biology: Core Concepts and Principles: MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary function of RNA within the cell according to molecular biology concepts?
o: Serving as the permanent genetic blueprint for all life
Facilitating cellular transcription and translation processes
Catalyzing all cellular metabolic reactions directly
Providing structural support and integrity for membranes
qs.e: RNA plays a critical role in the flow of genetic information from DNA to proteins by facilitating transcription and translation. DNA serves as the permanent blueprint of life rather than RNA.
qs.s: Molecular Biology: Core Concepts and Principles: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following techniques is specifically developed within molecular biology to study, separate, and manipulate biomolecules?
qs.e: PCR, electrophoresis, and chromatography are biomolecular techniques used to study and manipulate molecules. CT scanning and ECG are diagnostic imaging and physiological monitoring tools, not biomolecular techniques.
qs.s: Molecular Biology: Core Concepts and Principles: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is considered a primary focus area of biochemistry within molecular biology?
o: Investigating inheritance patterns and gene regulation
Analyzing anatomical macroscopic changes in embryos
Developing electrophoretic devices for hospital diagnostics
Exploring chemical reactions and molecular interactions
qs.e: Biochemistry explores the chemical reactions and molecular interactions sustaining life processes, whereas genetics focuses on inheritance and gene expression. Anatomical changes belong to gross morphology rather than biochemistry.
qs.s: Molecular Biology: Core Concepts and Principles: MCQs

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Molecular biology studies DNA, RNA and proteins to explain how cells store, copy and use genetic information. Clinicians use this knowledge to interpret genetic tests, understand pathogen mechanisms and guide targeted therapies.

sections.p: Molecular biology examines the flow of genetic information (DNA → RNA → protein) and how alterations cause disease.
b: Central dogma: DNA transcribed to RNA, translated to protein
Key molecules: DNA, mRNA, tRNA, ribosomes, polymerases

sections.p: Transcription copies a gene into messenger RNA; translation reads mRNA codons to assemble a protein chain.
b: RNA polymerase binds promoter → initiates transcription
Ribosome reads codons → tRNA delivers amino acids
Post‑translational modifications fine‑tune protein function

sections.p: Gene expression is controlled at multiple levels to match cellular needs and external signals.
b: Promoter/enhancer binding by transcription factors
RNA splicing, stability, and microRNA silencing
Feedback inhibition of enzymes

sections.p: Mutations, epigenetic changes or viral integration disrupt normal protein production, leading to disease.
b: Point mutations → sickle‑cell disease, thalassaemia
Gene deletions/duplications → Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Oncogenic viruses (HPV, EBV) insert oncogenes
Epigenetic silencing → tumor suppressor loss

sections.p: Molecular tests diagnose inherited disorders, identify infectious agents, and select targeted cancer therapies.
b: PCR for TB, HIV, malaria parasites
BRCA1/2 sequencing for breast‑cancer risk
CFTR mutation panel for cystic fibrosis
NGS panels for rare metabolic diseases

t.b: Confirms active TB when sputum smear is negative; a positive result guides anti‑TB therapy
Distinguishes sickle‑cell disease from other hemoglobinopathies; informs transfusion and hydroxyurea decisions
Identifies pathogenic variants; positive result triggers surveillance or prophylactic surgery

sections.p: Focus on the flow of genetic information, common mutation types, and the clinical use of molecular diagnostics.
b: Remember the Hershey‑Chase experiment proved DNA is the genetic material
Differentiate between loss‑of‑function and gain‑of‑function mutations
Know which test answers which clinical question (e.g., PCR = presence of pathogen DNA)

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive neurological decline with a known metabolic gene defect
Severe anemia in a child with suspected sickle‑cell disease
Unexplained fever in an immunocompromised patient with negative cultures – consider viral PCR

faq.q: Why do we test for viral DNA instead of antibodies in acute infection?
faq.a: DNA appears earlier than antibodies, allowing earlier diagnosis and treatment.

faq.q: What is the clinical impact of a silent mutation?
faq.a: Often no effect, but it can alter splicing or regulatory sites, causing disease.

faq.q: How does epigenetic silencing contribute to cancer?
faq.a: Methylation of tumor‑suppressor promoters shuts down their expression, promoting uncontrolled growth.
